power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Drug-resistant tuberculosis surveillance requires diagnostic systems that can rapidly identify resistance beyond rifampicin and generate potentially actionable resistance information for routine public-health monitoring.
We evaluated programmatic Xpert MTB/XDR use and characterized the molecular resistance profiles generated within a regional tuberculosis diagnostic network in northern Morocco.
We retrospectively analyzed 258 Xpert MTB/XDR testing episodes performed from April 2022 to July 2026 and linked available Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra results with target-level molecular outputs.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex was detected in 203 episodes (78.7%), of which 188 (92.6%) had an interpretable rifampicin result.

Molecular rifampicin resistance was detected in 75/188 episodes (39.9%) and isoniazid resistance in 71/192 (37.0%); molecular multidrug-resistant tuberculosis was identified in 51/184 (27.7%) episodes with paired results.

Among 186 episodes with interpretable rifampicin and additional resistance results, 75 (40.3%) had resistance to at least one additional drug class, including 21/112 (18.8%) rifampicin-susceptible and 54/74 (73.0%) rifampicinresistant episodes.

Among 92 resistant episodes with complete profiles, 66 (71.7%) showed resistance to two or more drug classes. rpoB3-and rpoB4-associated signals predominated among rifampicin-resistant episodes, katG-associated signals among isoniazid-resistant episodes, and gyrA targets among fluoroquinolone-resistant episodes.
Mixed wild-type and mutation-associated signals occurred across rpoB and gyrA.

These findings support the use of routine Xpert MTB/XDR testing as a component of regional drug-resistant tuberculosis surveillance, enabling systematic characterization of multiclass resistance and molecular resistance patterns within routine diagnostic networks.

Such molecular surveillance should be integrated with phenotypic susceptibility testing and genomic sequencing to resolve discordant, atypical, or clinically consequential profiles and build a more comprehensive regional resistance-monitoring system.
Tuberculosis (TB), caused by members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), remains a major global infectious disease threat.
In 2024, an estimated 10.7 million people developed TB globally, while 8.3 million were newly diagnosed and notified (1).
text.formatted: In 2024, an estimated 10.7 million people developed TB globally, while 8.3 million were newly diagnosed and notified <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: Despite progress in TB diagnosis and treatment, the global response remains off track to meet the End TB Strategy targets.
Drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) remains a major challenge for effective treatment and disease control (1) (2) (3).
text.formatted: Drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) remains a major challenge for effective treatment and disease control <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>.

text.text: Delayed detection of resistance can delay appropriate treatment, compromise patient management, and contribute to continued transmission.
Rapid and comprehensive drug-susceptibility testing is therefore an important component of both clinical decision-making and DR-TB surveillance (4) (5) (6).
text.formatted: Rapid and comprehensive drug-susceptibility testing is therefore an important component of both clinical decision-making and DR-TB surveillance <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref>.

text.text: Conventional culture-based drug-susceptibility testing (pDST) remains important for comprehensive resistance assessment but is limited by prolonged turnaround times and substantial laboratory requirements.

Rapid molecular diagnostics have consequently become central to the detection and surveillance of DR-TB, particularly in settings where timely resistance characterization is needed to guide treatment and strengthen programmatic monitoring (7).
text.formatted: Rapid molecular diagnostics have consequently become central to the detection and surveillance of DR-TB, particularly in settings where timely resistance characterization is needed to guide treatment and strengthen programmatic monitoring <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: Among the World Health Organization (WHO)-recommended molecular diagnostic tools, the GeneXpert platform is widely used for rapid detection of TB and drug resistance (8).
text.formatted: Among the World Health Organization (WHO)-recommended molecular diagnostic tools, the GeneXpert platform is widely used for rapid detection of TB and drug resistance <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>.

text.text: Xpert MTB/RIF substantially reduced the time required to detect MTBC and rifampicin resistance, while Xpert MTB/XDR expanded molecular resistance testing to additional drug classes, including isoniazid, FQs, second-line injectable agents, and ethionamide.
The assay interrogates resistance-associated targets including katG, inhA, fabG1, gyrA, gyrB, rrs, and eis sequences (8) (9) (10).
text.formatted: The assay interrogates resistance-associated targets including katG, inhA, fabG1, gyrA, gyrB, rrs, and eis sequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref>.

text.text: This expanded molecular coverage can provide more comprehensive resistance information within routine diagnostic workflows and generate target-level data that may be useful for laboratory-based surveillance.

However, Xpert MTB/XDR remains a targeted assay and does not capture all genetic mechanisms of resistance; consequently, it cannot replace comprehensive phenotypic DST or genomic characterization when broader resistance assessment is required (11, 12).
text.formatted: However, Xpert MTB/XDR remains a targeted assay and does not capture all genetic mechanisms of resistance; consequently, it cannot replace comprehensive phenotypic DST or genomic characterization when broader resistance assessment is required <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond binary resistance classification, routine molecular diagnostics can generate targetassociated profiles that describe the distribution and co-occurrence of resistance and provide additional information for molecular surveillance.
Integrating rifampicin-associated rpoB . profiles (Xpert MTB/RIFUltra) testing with Xpert MTB/XDR data can therefore provide a multidimensional view of DR-TB within routine diagnostic networks.

Such data may help characterize resistance patterns at the regional level and identify molecular signal variability that warrants further investigation, particularly in settings where systematic genomic surveillance remains limited (13, 14).
text.formatted: Such data may help characterize resistance patterns at the regional level and identify molecular signal variability that warrants further investigation, particularly in settings where systematic genomic surveillance remains limited <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14)</ref>.

text.text: In Morocco, previous studies have identified recurrent resistance-associated variants in rpoB, katG, inhA, and gyrA, including established markers of rifampicin and isoniazid resistance (MDR-TB) (15) (16) (17) (18).
text.formatted: In Morocco, previous studies have identified recurrent resistance-associated variants in rpoB, katG, inhA, and gyrA, including established markers of rifampicin and isoniazid resistance (MDR-TB) <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref>.

text.text: Studies from northern Morocco have also documented MDR-TB and recurrent rpoB profiles (19, 20).
text.formatted: Studies from northern Morocco have also documented MDR-TB and recurrent rpoB profiles <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20)</ref>.

text.text: However, Moroccan evidence has largely been generated from selected clinical or reference-laboratory populations and has focused on line-probe assays, targeted sequencing, or other molecular approaches (21) (22) (23) (24) (25) (26) (27).
text.formatted: However, Moroccan evidence has largely been generated from selected clinical or reference-laboratory populations and has focused on line-probe assays, targeted sequencing, or other molecular approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(21)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(23)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(26)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27)</ref>.

text.text: Although Xpert MTB/XDR has been incorporated into Morocco's 2024-2030 TB strategic plan for expanded resistance detection alongside phenotypic DST and sequencing (28), evidence from its routine programmatic use and the broader resistance information it generates remains limited.
text.formatted: Although Xpert MTB/XDR has been incorporated into Morocco's 2024-2030 TB strategic plan for expanded resistance detection alongside phenotypic DST and sequencing <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref>, evidence from its routine programmatic use and the broader resistance information it generates remains limited.

text.text: We therefore conducted a retrospective study of routine Xpert MTB/XDR testing from its implementation in April 2022 through July 2026 within a regional TB diagnostic network in northern Morocco.

We characterized programmatic testing outcomes and molecular resistance profiles, integrating rifampicin resistance and rpoB target data from linked Xpert MTB/RIFUltra results with Xpert MTB/XDR resistance-associated targets.

We further assessed resistance combinations, target-level molecular patterns, and melting-temperature and melt-peak characteristics to evaluate the potential of routinely generated molecular data to strengthen regional DR-TB surveillance.
We conducted a retrospective, laboratory-based observational study of routine Xpert MTB/XDR testing at the Center of TB Diagnosis and Respiratory Diseases, Tétouan, Morocco.
The laboratory served the Tangier-Tétouan-Al Hoceima (TTA) administrative region (northern Morocco), encompassing its eight prefectures and provinces (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: The laboratory served the Tangier-Tétouan-Al Hoceima (TTA) administrative region (northern Morocco), encompassing its eight prefectures and provinces (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">1</ref>).

text.text: Xpert MTB/XDR was introduced in 2022 within the regional TB diagnostic network and was used for patients with rifampicin resistance or other predefined indicators of increased drug-resistance risk, including . previous treatment or retreatment, known or suspected drug-resistant tuberculosis exposure, persistent acid-fast bacillus positivity after the fifth month of treatment, or the need for expanded resistance characterization to inform treatment planning.
The retrospective dataset did not permit quantification of the indication-specific contribution of each referral criterion.
All Xpert MTB/XDR assay records generated at the laboratory from April 2022 through July 2026 were eligible.
No assay was excluded on the basis of final result.
Target-level resistance analyses were restricted to MTB-detected episodes with interpretable results for the corresponding target/class.
Because GeneXpert timestamps were inconsistently recorded, dates were used only for record linkage and identification of testing episodes, not temporal analyses.
Xpert MTB/XDR records were linked, where available, to Xpert MTB/RIF-Ultra results using patient and sample identifiers.
Age, sex, and referral address were obtained from routine laboratory registers.

Each assay run was considered a testing episode; five repeat assays were performed after initially invalid results and yielded interpretable results, and these repeats were retained as separate episodes to characterize the programmatic testing pathway.
For outcome-specific analyses, the subsequent interpretable result was used, whereas the preceding invalid assay was excluded from the corresponding denominator.
Potential duplicates were assessed using patient, sample, and testing information.
Xpert MTB/XDR and Xpert MTB/RIF-Ultra testing were performed according to the manufacturer's instructions and routine procedures using the GeneXpert system (Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) (28).
text.formatted: Xpert MTB/XDR and Xpert MTB/RIF-Ultra testing were performed according to the manufacturer's instructions and routine procedures using the GeneXpert system (Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref>.

text.text: Final interpretations and available target-level parameters, including cycle threshold (Ct), endpoint fluorescence (EndPt), amplification result, melting temperature (Tm), and melt-peak height, were retained.
Targets included inhA, katG, fabG1, and ahpC for isoniazid resistance; inhA for ethionamide resistance; gyrA1-3 and gyrB2 for fluoroquinolones; and rrs and eis for second-line injectable resistance.

Linked Xpert MTB/RIF-Ultra records provided rifampicin results and available rpoB1-4 data, including Ct, EndPt, amplification results, and wild-type-or mutation-associated Tm and meltpeak measurements.
Melt-curve signals were treated as assay-level characteristics and were not interpreted as specific nucleotide substitutions without an established assay-specific interpretation.
Resistance classifications were based on final molecular assay interpretations.
Molecular MDR-TB was defined as concurrent rifampicin and isoniazid resistance.
Resistance variables were coded as detected, not detected, or indeterminate/missing.
Resistance combinations were derived for rifampicin, isoniazid, fluoroquinolones, ethionamide, and second-line injectable agents (amikacin, kanamycin, and capreomycin).
Complete-profile analyses included episodes with interpretable results across all assessed resistance classes.
The number of resistant drug classes and distinct resistance-associated molecular targets was calculated per episode; multiple signals within the same target were counted once.
All final Xpert MTB/XDR outcomes were retained, including MTB detected, MTB not detected, invalid, and no result.
The primary denominator was all testing episodes; outcomespecific analyses used the relevant interpretable denominator, and non-interpretable results were not classified as susceptible.
Programmatic indicators included MTB detection, availability of linked rifampicin results, resistance by drug class, resistance combinations, and number of resistant classes.
Molecular profiles integrated categorical resistance interpretations with target-level data, including resistance-associated targets and combined rpoB/Xpert MTB/XDR profiles.
For exploratory quantitative molecular analyses, all available numeric Tm and melt-peak measurements were retained and classified as WT or mutation-associated.
Mixed WT/mutation signals were both retained.
Thus, the unit of analysis was the assay-level molecular signal rather than the patient or testing episode.
Tm and peak-height distributions were summarized as median (IQR) and compared between signal groups.
Tm and melt-peak distributions were compared between wild-type and mutation-associated signal groups using non-parametric tests, as appropriate, without assigning specific nucleotide substitutions.
Missing, invalid, no-result, and non-interpretable results were distinguished from negative results and were not imputed.
When an invalid assay was repeated, the subsequent interpretable result was retained for the relevant analysis, while the initial assay remained classified as invalid.
Analyses used the relevant interpretable denominator.
Raw GeneXpert exports were reviewed for duplicates, formatting inconsistencies, missing values, and implausible measurements.
Final interpretations were cross-checked against analyte-level results, and records with uncertain patient or specimen linkage were excluded from linkage-based analyses.
The study used retrospectively collected routine laboratory and clinical data without additional intervention or specimen collection.
Identifiable information was used only for internal linkage and removed from the analytical dataset.

A total of 258 Xpert MTB/XDR testing episodes were analyzed.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) was detected in 203 (78.7%); 28 (10.9%) were MTBC-not-detected, 16 (6.2%) had no result, six (2.3%) were initially invalid, five of which were repeated and yielded interpretable results included among the 203 MTBC-detected episodes, and five (1.9%) lacked a final interpretation.
Across all testing episodes, 201 (77.9%) involved men and 57 (22.1%) women; age was available for 253 episodes, with a median of 39 years (IQR, 30-49).
Most specimens were sputum (94.2%), and referrals originated from seven prefecture/province categories, with Tétouan and Tangier accounting for 61.6% of all episodes.
These distributions reflect the referral composition of the testing network rather than population-level estimates.
A linked, interpretable rifampicin result was available for 188/203 MTB-detected episodes (92.6%), including 75 (39.9%) rifampicin-resistant episodes.

text.text: Among 184 episodes with paired interpretable RIF and INH results, 51 (27.7%) showed concurrent resistance, corresponding to a molecular MDR-TB profile.

Among 186 episodes with an interpretable rifampicin result and at least one additional resistance result, 75 (40.3%) had resistance to at least one additional drug class, including 18.8% of rifampicin-susceptible and 73.0% of rifampicin-resistant episodes.

Additional isoniazid resistance was strongly associated with rifampicin resistance (OR, 12.13; P<0.0001), as was ethionamide resistance (OR, 4.47; P=0.0014), whereas fluoroquinolone resistance was not significantly associated with rifampicin resistance (OR, 1.99; P=0.155) (Table 3).

Among 50 molecular MDR-TB episodes with interpretable FQ and ETH results, 15 (30.0%) had MDR+ETH, seven (14.0%) MDR+FQ, and one (2.0%) MDR+FQ+ETH.
FQ resistance was not significantly more frequent in MDR than non-MDR episodes (16.0% versus 9.0%; OR, 1.92; Fisher's exact P=0.190), whereas ETH resistance occurred in 16/50 (32.0%) MDR episodes.

text.text: The emergence of DR-TB has shifted the diagnostic challenge from MTBC detection to rapid resistance profiling for treatment and surveillance (29).

text.text: However, molecular testing in many resource-limited settings remains focused on rifampicin, with broader profiling largely restricted to selected cohorts or research settings.
In Morocco, resistance has similarly been characterized mainly through pDST, rpoB sequencing, and line-probe assays in selected populations (15, 16, 18-20, 27, 30, 31).

text.text: In the present setting, Xpert MTB/XDR was introduced through a targeted workflow for patients with rifampicin resistance or other indicators of increased drug-resistance risk, including previous treatment or exposure and persistent acidfast bacilli positivity after the fifth month of treatment.
To our knowledge, this is the first Moroccan study to characterize multidimensional resistance information from routine Xpert MTB/XDR.
Across 258 testing episodes over four years of implementation in northern Morocco, MTBC was detected in 203 (78.7%), while only a subset produced invalid, no-result, or noninterpretable outcomes.

These findings highlight that the public-health value of molecular surveillance depends not only on resistance detection but also on specimen quality, result validity, repeat testing, and management of unresolved assays (32, 33).

text.text: As a targeted assay within the diagnostic pathway, its effectiveness depends essentially on workflows that accommodate invalid, indeterminate, and repeat results (9, 34).

text.text: The expanded resistance panel identified additional resistance in 40.3% of episodes with interpretable rifampicin and additional resistance results, including 18.8% of rifampicinsusceptible and 73.0% of rifampicin-resistant episodes.
This illustrates the value of broader molecular testing for identifying resistance that would not be captured by rifampicin-focused testing alone (7, 36, 37).

text.text: Reflex Xpert MTB/XDR testing can provide a broader molecular resistance profile within a single workflow, complementing pDST and enabling more complete initial characterization.
The composition of additional resistance was drug-class specific.
Isoniazid resistance was strongly associated with rifampicin resistance (OR, 12.13; p<0.0001), consistent with the molecular basis of MDR-TB (38).

Moroccan studies similarly report a substantial MDR burden among rifampicin-resistant isolates, but more heterogeneous second-line resistance across cohorts (19, 20, 30, 31, 39).

Although these findings cannot be directly compared with studies based on selected MDR-TB cohorts or different testing methods (30, 31, 39), they indicate substantial multiclass resistance within the tested population.

text.text: Given the referral-based design and lack of adjustment for potential confounding, our finding should be considered exploratory rather than an independent association.
Ethionamide resistance also varied across provinces, although sparse strata limit interpretation.
These findings are therefore hypothesis-generating and warrant confirmation in population-based studies using adjusted analyses.

Together, these findings position Xpert MTB/XDR not only as a resistance diagnostic assay but as a potential component of regional DR-TB surveillance by generating resistance-class profiles, target-associated signatures, and quantitative molecular data within single routine workflows.

This study has several limitations.

Its retrospective, laboratory-based design reflects referral and testing selection rather than population-based sampling; therefore, estimates apply to the tested population rather than northern Morocco as a whole.
Variable class-specific denominators also limited comparisons across resistance classes and inference on uniquepatient burden.
The absence of complete phenotypic and genomic reference data limited assessment of molecular-phenotypic discordance, off-target mechanisms, heteroresistance, and borderline resistance (45, 66, 74).
The small number of injectable-resistant episodes and lack of treatment and clinical outcome data further limited interpretation.
Thus, the study describes programmatic molecular resistance epidemiology rather than overall resistance prevalence, transmission dynamics, or treatment impact.

In conclusion, four years of routine Xpert MTB/XDR testing in northern Morocco demonstrate how expanded molecular diagnostics can transform routine laboratory testing into structured DR-TB surveillance data.

By integrating rifampicin classification with additional resistance classes, multidrug profiles, target-associated signals, and quantitative assay features, routine diagnostic networks can generate broader information on the regional resistance landscape.

The frequency of additional and multiclass resistance supports the value of broader resistance characterization, while the limitations of targeted assays highlight the need to integrate molecular, phenotypic, and genomic approaches.

Such complementary strategies can strengthen resistance monitoring and provide a practical framework for developing more . comprehensive DR-TB surveillance systems, particularly in settings where genomic surveillance remains limited.
